title: Bony Pelvis Anatomy
descriptor: Hip Bones, Sacrum & Coccyx, Joints, True & False Pelvis, Fractures & Pelvic Girdle Pain
intro: The bony pelvis is made up of the two hip bones together with the sacrum and the coccyx. The hip bones link each lower limb to the base of the spine, and the pelvis supports the weight of the upper body and passes it on to the lower limbs. The pelvic cavity inside it houses the urinary bladder, rectum and internal reproductive organs, which the pelvic girdle helps to protect.

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Two hip bones, the sacrum and the coccyx

keyFacts.label: Each hip bone
keyFacts.value: Formed from the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse during the late teenage years

keyFacts.label: Joints
keyFacts.value: Pubic symphysis at the front, sacroiliac joints at the back and the sacrococcygeal joint between sacrum and coccyx

keyFacts.label: Divisions
keyFacts.value: False (greater) pelvis above the pelvic brim and true (lesser) pelvis below it

keyFacts.label: Landmarks
keyFacts.value: Iliac crest, ischial spine, ischial tuberosity, obturator foramen and acetabulum

keyFacts.label: Function
keyFacts.value: Supports the upper body, passes its weight to the lower limbs and helps to protect the pelvic organs

keyFacts.label: Investigation
keyFacts.value: X-ray, with CT to assess the pelvis and detect bleeding after injury

sections.heading: The hip bone
sections.body: The hip bone, also called the coxal bone, is the single bone that makes up the pelvic girdle and links each lower limb to the base of the spine. Each adult hip bone is formed from three bones, the ilium, ischium and pubis, which are separate in early life and fuse during the late teenage years. The ilium is the upper, fan-shaped and largest part, and its curved upper margin is the iliac crest. The ischium forms the posteroinferior part and bears the ischial tuberosity, a large roughened area that carries the weight of the body when sitting. The pubis forms the anterior part and curves medially to join the pubis of the opposite hip bone at the pubic symphysis. Where the three bones converge on the outer side of each hip bone they form the acetabulum, a deep cup-shaped socket that is part of the hip joint.

sections.heading: Landmarks and muscle attachments
sections.body: The iliac crest ends in front at the anterior superior iliac spine, with a rounded anterior inferior iliac spine just below it, and curves downwards behind to end as the posterior superior iliac spine. On the back edge of the ilium the greater sciatic notch lies above the ischial spine, a pointed projection that separates it from the lesser sciatic notch. The obturator foramen is a large opening in the lower front of the hip bone, bounded by the ischium and pubis. The ischial tuberosity gives attachment to hip and thigh muscles, including the hamstrings, and the pelvic floor muscles attach along the lower edges of the pubis.

sections.heading: Sacrum, coccyx, joints and ligaments
sections.body: The midline sacrum and coccyx complete the bony pelvis. At the front the two hip bones meet at the pubic symphysis, and at the back each hip bone unites with the sacrum at a sacroiliac joint. The coccyx attaches to the sacrum at the sacrococcygeal joint. The anterior, posterior and interosseous sacroiliac ligaments connect the sacrum and ilium and stabilise the joint. The sacroiliac joint is supplied by several arteries, including the iliolumbar, superior gluteal and lateral sacral arteries. The sacrotuberous ligament runs from the sacrum to the ischial tuberosity, and the sacrospinous ligament is a triangular band from the ischial spine to the sacrum and coccyx. Together these two ligaments form the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, and the pudendal vessels and nerves pass between them.

sections.heading: The true and false pelvis
sections.body: The pelvic brim, also called the pelvic inlet, separates the true pelvis from the false pelvis above it. It runs from the sacral promontory across the iliopectineal line to the pubic symphysis, and it is formed by the pectineal line of the pubis, the arcuate line of the ilium and the ala of the sacrum. The broad false (greater) pelvis lies above the brim, is formed by the wings of the ilium and belongs to the abdomen. The narrower true (lesser) pelvis lies below the brim and is bounded below by the pelvic outlet, which is bounded by the coccyx, the ischial tuberosities and the pubic symphysis. The true pelvis holds the bladder, rectum and part of the descending colon, and also the uterus, fallopian tubes and ovaries in people who have them.

sections.heading: Shape differences between pelvises
sections.body: OpenStax describes the adult female pelvic inlet as round or oval and the male inlet as heart-shaped. The female sacrum is described as wider, shorter and less curved, with a sacral promontory that projects less into the pelvic cavity, which accounts for the rounder inlet. The female lesser pelvis is described as wider and shallower and the male lesser pelvis as narrower and deeper, and the subpubic angle is larger in the female pelvis. The greater sciatic notch is narrower and deeper in the male hip bone than the broader notch of the female hip bone, and male pelvic bones are described as thicker and heavier. The female pelvis is wider overall, which relates to childbirth.

sections.heading: Function and blood supply
sections.body: The pelvis mainly supports the upper body and passes its weight to the lower limbs. StatPearls describes the bony pelvis as a junction between the forces of the spine and of the lower limbs during movement. Each hip bone forms a basin that supports the trunk and anchors muscles and ligaments of the lower limb. The pelvic girdle also helps to protect the pelvic and abdominopelvic organs. During childbirth the pelvic outlet offers support and guidance for the foetus through the birth canal. The internal iliac artery supplies the pelvic organs, the perineal floor and the gluteal muscles.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body:
A fracture of the pubic rami, which make up the pubis at the front of the pelvis, most often follows a fall from standing, particularly in older people whose bones are weakened by osteoporosis. NHS trust leaflets describe pain that increases with movement and weight bearing, and say that a fracture of this kind is usually managed without surgery. In injuries that disrupt the pelvic ring, the posterior pelvic venous plexus is the main source of haemorrhage.

A hip fracture is a different injury, a break in the upper thigh bone close to the hip joint, usually caused by a fall or a blow to the side of the hip.

Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy is described by NHS trusts as uncomfortable symptoms caused by stiffness of the pelvic joints, or the joints moving unevenly, at the back or front of the pelvis. The pain may spread to the hips, groin, thighs or lower back, and people with significant symptoms are advised to speak to a midwife or GP.

sections.heading: How the pelvis is investigated
sections.body: For a suspected hip fracture, clinicians usually start with the symptoms, a physical examination and the history of the injury, and an X-ray usually confirms the diagnosis, with a CT scan occasionally used. CT is also useful for assessing the pelvis and detecting bleeding after pelvic injury, and clinicians rule out chest and abdominal sources of bleeding before attributing it to the pelvis. An X-ray is a quick, painless test that produces images of the inside of the body; the person needs to keep still, and more than one image may be taken from different angles.
